props.title: Ginger Snaps
props.initialSlug: Sisters face deadly changes during a werewolf curse

sections.content: Ginger Snaps (2000) revolutionized werewolf horror by explicitly linking lycanthropy with female puberty and sisterhood. The film follows the Fitzgerald sisters - death-obsessed outcasts Brigitte and Ginger - as the latter's werewolf transformation parallels her sexual awakening. Like Carrie (1976) before it, the film weaponizes feminine biology into horror, but adds layers of complicated sisterly devotion and rage against suburban conformity. Director John Fawcett crafts a savage critique of coming-of-age expectations while delivering genuine scares and practical effects that hold up remarkably well.

sections.content: The film sparked a wave of female-centered horror that explored themes of bodily transformation and sexual awakening through genre elements. Jennifer's Body (2009) borrowed heavily from its template of best friends torn apart by monstrous change, while The Witch (2015) similarly focused on a young woman's power being demonized by society. Even non-horror films like Thirteen (2003) echo Ginger Snaps' unflinching look at female adolescence through a dark lens.

The practical werewolf effects in Ginger Snaps deserve special attention, following in the tradition of An American Werewolf in London (1981) and The Howling (1981). Rather than relying on CGI, the gradual transformation uses prosthetics and makeup to create a viscerally unsettling metamorphosis that serves the story's themes of body horror and alienation. This approach influenced later films like Dog Soldiers (2002) and Late Phases (2014). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence on Horror

sections.content: The film spawned two direct sequels - Ginger Snaps 2: Unleashed (2004) and Ginger Snaps Back: The Beginning (2004) - but its greater legacy lies in how it helped legitimize horror as a vehicle for serious feminist discourse. Films like A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night (2014) and Raw (2016) follow its lead in using monster tropes to explore female experience. The success of Ginger Snaps also paved the way for more Canadian horror, influencing filmmakers like David Cronenberg's daughter Caitlin Cronenberg and the Soska Sisters.
